title: “SONG OF SOLOMON IS IN YOUR BIBLE—AND YES, IT’S ABOUT DESIRE”
paragraphs:
“SONG OF SOLOMON IS IN YOUR BIBLE—AND YES, IT’S ABOUT DESIRE”
The Book Christians Sometimes Whisper About May Be Exposing Something the Church Was Never Supposed to Make You Ashamed Of
There is a book in your Bible that begins with a woman wanting to be kissed.
Not after twelve paragraphs of theological explanation.
Not after apologizing for having a body.
She wants the man she loves to kiss her.
God allowed those words to remain in Holy Scripture.
That should make some of us uncomfortable.
Not because Scripture has become inappropriate.
Perhaps because somewhere along the way, we became uncomfortable with something God was never embarrassed to create.
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ כִּי־טוֹבִים דֹּדֶיךָ מִיָּיִן
Yishaqeni minneshiqot pihu, ki-tovim dodekha miyyayin.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, for your love is better than wine.”
And before somebody tries to rescue God from the awkwardness by immediately saying, “Well, obviously that is only symbolic of Christ and the Church…”
There is something beautiful here that we may miss when we become more embarrassed about human desire than the Bible itself appears to be.

Song of Songs certainly developed a long and beautiful history of spiritual interpretation. Jewish interpreters saw in it the covenant love between God and Israel. Christian interpreters have often heard echoes of Christ’s love for His people.
Those readings can teach us something precious.
But the poem itself speaks unapologetically about human lovers.
Because some Christians were taught only two ways to think about desire.
Either pretend you do not have it…
or feel ashamed because you do.
So the unmarried believer feels attraction and immediately wonders whether something is spiritually wrong with them.
The married couple slowly stops talking about intimacy because “holy people” apparently aren't supposed to need those conversations.
The teenager discovers desire and receives plenty of warnings about sexual sin but almost no theology explaining why the desire exists in the first place.
The person recovering from pornography begins to believe that victory means becoming incapable of attraction.
The believer carrying sexual regret starts thinking purity means becoming a person without a past.
And into all that confusion sits this strange, beautiful, almost startling little book of the Bible.
As though God is reminding us:
Genesis establishes that foundation before humanity falls. A man is joined to his wife, and the two become one flesh. Scripture even tells us that they were naked and unashamed.
Before people learned to use one another.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of God rescuing souls from the terrible inconvenience of having bodies.
Christianity proclaims something far more astonishing.
Jesus Christ entered our embodied humanity.
Christian hope is not the abandonment of creation but its redemption.
So perhaps the question is not, “How do I kill every desire inside me?”
What does Jesus want to redeem, reorder, and rule inside me?
Song of Songs understands both the fire and the boundary.
הִשְׁבַּעְתִּי אֶתְכֶם בְּנוֹת יְרוּשָׁלִַם... אִם־תָּעִירוּ וְאִם־תְּעוֹרְרוּ אֶת־הָאַהֲבָה עַד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּץ
Hishba‘ti etkhem benot Yerushalayim… im-ta‘iru ve’im-te‘oreru et-ha’ahavah ‘ad sheteḥpatz.
“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem… do not awaken or arouse love until it pleases.”
That warning appears repeatedly through the Song.
Do not awaken love before its proper time.
What a sentence for our generation.
We live inside an economy designed to awaken desire constantly.
Hookup culture offers bodies without permanence.
Advertising survives by convincing you that satisfaction is one purchase away.
Social media can turn people into images before we remember they are souls.
And Scripture whispers something profoundly countercultural:
Do not play carelessly with desire.
Later, Song of Songs describes love with language of extraordinary intensity:
“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death…”
Its flashes are flashes of fire.
Fire inside a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire across the living-room floor can destroy it.
The problem isn't that fire exists.
The question is whether that fire is rightly ordered.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been burned.
Maybe you learned intimacy through pornography before anyone taught you covenant.
Maybe someone introduced you to sexuality before you were ready.
Maybe somebody violated boundaries that should have protected you.
Maybe you gave yourself to somebody who promised forever and disappeared when forever became inconvenient.
Maybe you're single and exhausted from pretending loneliness never hurts.
Maybe you're attracted to someone you know you cannot righteously have.
Maybe your browser history and your Sunday worship history look like they belong to two different people.
Until eventually you stop asking whether Jesus can forgive you and start wondering whether He is simply tired of you.
This is where the Gospel becomes more than religious vocabulary.
Jesus did not come merely to improve respectable people.
People carrying memories they wish could be erased.
And Christ does something far greater than pretending the scandal never happened.
He carries sin to the cross.
The Gospel does not say sexual sin is harmless.
It says Christ's blood is powerful.
The Gospel does not rename darkness as light.
It brings darkness into the light where grace can finally do its work.
Paul could write to believers in Corinth after naming devastating patterns of sexual immorality and say:
Not because they suddenly acquired spotless histories.
But history no longer had the authority to name them.
Justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
Not pretending there was never a scandal.
Grace rewriting what the scandal was allowed to become.
Grace does not mean God approves everything you desire.
Grace means you no longer have to hide your desires from God.
Some desires must be celebrated within God's design.
Some must be starved because feeding them is destroying us.
Some wounds beneath our desires need healing.
Some secret sins need confession and repentance.
But none of them become safer because we hide them from Jesus.
You cannot shock the One who already knew everything when He went to the cross.
You cannot confess something that makes Christ suddenly discover who you really are.
Still He defended the disgraced without pretending sin did not matter.
Still He told sinners to leave sin behind.
Still He stretched His arms across wood.
This is why biblical purity is far more beautiful than merely saying “no.”
Christian purity is learning to say a greater yes.
Yes to seeing another person's body as belonging to a person made in God's image rather than as material for your consumption.
Yes to refusing to turn somebody else's daughter, son, husband, wife, future spouse, loneliness, weakness, or vulnerability into fuel for your appetite.
Yes to repentance when you fail.
Yes to marriage as a covenant rather than merely a romantic mood.
Yes to letting Christ teach your desires that they are servants, not kings.
Because your desires make terrible gods.
They promise freedom and often create chains.
He loves you without consuming you.
He knows you without exploiting you.
He sees everything without humiliating you.
He commands you without using you.
He corrects you without discarding you.
And He can satisfy a depth in you that another human being was never created to fill.
This is where Song of Songs and the Gospel must be related carefully.
The lovers in Song of Songs are not simply code words we are required to replace with “Jesus” and “the Church” in every verse.
The poem celebrates human love with its own God-given dignity.
But precisely because human love is good, it can point beyond itself.
Every good gift ultimately reminds us that we are creatures, not gods.
Having somebody choose you cannot save you.
Your spouse cannot carry the weight of being your Messiah.
And if you demand that another human being heal the deepest fracture between you and God, eventually you will crush them beneath expectations they were never created to bear.
Only Christ can reconcile sinners to God.
Only Christ can take guilt and actually answer it.
Only Christ can enter the grave and come back carrying victory.
Only Christ can give the disgraced a new name.
Only Christ can transform not merely what we do but what we increasingly learn to love.
And maybe that is where this becomes painfully personal.
What are you asking desire to give you?
To feel alive for fifteen minutes?
Sometimes the behavior everybody sees is only smoke.
Jesus wants to reach the fire underneath it.
Repentance is not merely saying, “God, make the consequences disappear.”
It is turning toward Christ and saying:
“Jesus, I don't want this thing to rule me anymore.
Even when I still want it…
Teach me how to want what is good.”
There may be nights when obedience feels less like victory music and more like deleting a number.
Walking away while every emotion tells you to stay.
Admitting that what you called “love” was actually dependency.
Admitting that what you called “freedom” has become slavery.
Admitting that what you called “just looking” has been training your heart to consume people.
Admitting that the wound is deeper than the habit.
And discovering that Jesus is waiting beneath the confession.
That is the breathtaking scandal of grace.
The hands qualified to condemn are the hands that were pierced.
And those scars do not make sin small.
Song of Songs is not permission to worship desire.
It is proof that Scripture does not need to pretend desire does not exist.
The Bible can celebrate embodied marital love without surrendering holiness.
It can speak about longing without becoming pornography.
It can honor attraction without turning human beings into products.
Perhaps some of us need to stop being ashamed that we experience desire…
and start becoming serious about where we take it.
Bring the thing you have never said aloud because you were afraid Christians would look at you differently.
The question is whether you will finally stop hiding.
If this exposed something you've been carrying silently, you don't need to tell strangers every detail. But you can make one honest declaration:
Somebody else reading the comments may discover they are not the only Christian still fighting.
And if somebody came into your mind while reading this, don't dismiss that.
Better yet, send this privately when the struggle is personal.
There may be a married couple who needs it.
A teenager asking questions nobody answers well.
A single Christian exhausted by shame.
A person convinced their sexual past permanently disqualified them from being deeply loved by God.
Not because giving money purchases blessing.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ.
Do not leave this article merely thinking differently about Song of Songs.
Your desire is not stronger than His lordship.
Your temptation is not stronger than His Spirit.
Your history is not stronger than His blood.
Your shame is not stronger than His grace.
Your failure is not stronger than His cross.
And your grave will not be stronger than His resurrection.
Maybe you came here because the title mentioned desire.
Maybe you stayed because somewhere between the Hebrew poetry and your own memories, this stopped being an article about an ancient love song.
If so, don't run from what you saw.
Receive forgiveness where Christ has promised forgiveness.
Seek accountability where secrecy has been feeding bondage.
And when you fail, don't make peace with the mud simply because you fell into it again.
Because the Savior who transforms sinners is still writing stories.
Especially the ones everybody assumed were finished.
And perhaps the line you need to carry with you tonight is this:
Jesus is not asking you to become less human; He is teaching every part of your humanity—including your deepest desires—how to come home under His lordship.
Because when Christ gets the final word, your worst chapter doesn't get to name the book.
